title: Mudita as a subject
hookLine: someone gets the thing you wanted; is what shows up under the congratulations envy, or a turning away?
tomorrow: how does a parent love a grown kid busy with their own life?

cards: A friend gets the thing you wanted: the part, the spot, the yes. The congratulations type out fine, and then something else shows up under them. What is it?
Buddhists name it two ways. The Visuddhimagga says gladness has a far enemy called arati: aversion, discontent, turning away from someone else's good news. Some modern teachers put it more bluntly.
The opposite of gladness, they say, is envy.

teach.b: Let the manual speak first. Mudita, gladness at someone else's good fortune, has a far enemy, arati, and the word is wide on purpose.
It catches envy, yes, but also the flat, bored turning away, the good for them with the eyes rolled, the change of subject.
It also names a near enemy: a giddy excitement about the good fortune itself, the stuff, which looks like gladness and isn't. Now let the modern teachers speak.
Their case: people live inside comparison, and the sting they actually meet is envy. Naming it plainly lets someone see it, hold it, and practice right next to it. Both sides keep the same practice.
The manual says to start where it's easy: a very dear friend whose good news is simple to love.
Hear it, and let the gladness come: how good, how glad they are. Then widen to someone neutral, then someone hostile. Gladness, in both readings, isn't a feeling you fake.
It's a muscle you train, starting light.

how: Sympathetic joy is the third of the four boundless states in Buddhist practice; in the Visuddhimagga's method it begins with a dear friend's good fortune and widens to neutral and hostile people.

games.q: what does “mudita as a subject” mean?
o: gladness at someone else's good fortune
pride in your own success and wins
a quiet joy found only in solitude

games.q: gladness and its enemies — tap the pairs.
p: the manual's far enemy: turning away

s: real gladness for someone means feeling no sting at all
both readings treat gladness as trained, starting light; it can be practiced right next to the sting.
in the Visuddhimagga, gladness's far enemy is arati, aversion or discontent
some modern teachers name envy instead; the manual's word is wider, a turning away.
mudita practice starts with the person whose win hurts most
it starts with a dear friend whose good news is easy to love.

games.q: your friend says the opposite of being glad for someone is envy, period. she asks for the old manual's best case. what's fair?
o: Buddhist texts don't talk about envy at all, so it isn't the opposite.
its far enemy is arati, turning away, which covers envy and the bored eye-roll too.
gladness has no enemy; it comes easily once you decide to feel it.
games.why: that's the manual at its strongest: arati is wide, envy plus the flat turning away. her view has a strong case too: envy is what people meet most plainly, and naming it helps.

practice: Count three pieces of good news that happened to other people lately, starting with someone it's easy to be glad for. For each one, say inwardly: good for you, may it last.
When you reach a harder one, stay a few breaths, and let even a little gladness count.

wordCard.voice: Mudita as a subject: gladness at someone else's good fortune, made the object of meditation, trained from the easy cases outward.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: gladness, joy at someone else's good fortune.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: gladness, even right next to the sting. Thirty-one of forty, finished.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 9 (gladness, mudita: begin with a very dear companion who is happy; then neutral and hostile persons; near enemy joy based on the home life, far enemy aversion, arati)
